# Question 1: Exploring Risk and Uncertainty

*Write-up* (Report) can be found at `Questions/Question1/Question1.pdf`

```{r}
# Functions for this question:
list.files('Questions/Question1/code/', full.names = T, recursive = T) %>% .[grepl('.R', .)] %>% as.list() %>% walk(~source(.))
```

## Data

I only load the data I ended up using for this question.

```{r Q1_data}
Idx_Daily  <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/Index_Returns_Daily.rds")
MSCI <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/MSCI_Indexes.rds")
Uncertainty <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/Econ_Uncertainty_Indexes.rds")
SafeCore <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/SafeCore.rds")
Stocks <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/Stock_Returns_Daily.rds")
Cons <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/Index_Constituents.rds")
Factor_Scores <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/Factor_Scores.rds")
```

## Part A 

My first thought was that Part A can really be further divided into two parts. These parts are whether volatility has gone up, and whether it moves with offshore markets. So I needed both local and global series on the same footing. 

For the local market I used the Capped SWIX (J433), since it is the broad market index and also SafeCore's benchmark. I added the Mid Cap (J201) and Small Cap (J202) indexes because I wanted to see whether any increase was only in the large companies or across the whole market. For global markets I used MSCI World (developed markets) and MSCI Emerging Markets, since South Africa is usually grouped with emerging markets. I first converted the MSCI data to daily returns (since it is in levels) and I started everything in 2015 because that is where the local data starts.

```{r Q1_A_Rets}
Local_Rets <-
  Idx_Daily %>%
  filter(Tickers %in% c("J433", "J201", "J202"))

Global_Rets <-
  MSCI %>%
  filter(Ticker %in% c("MXWO Index", "MXEF Index")) %>%
  Q1_Level_to_Returns() %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20150101))

Eq_Rets <- bind_rows(Local_Rets, Global_Rets)
```

I started with a rolling standard deviation to see how volatility changes through time. I chose a 63 day window (about three months) because it matches the three month horizon of the currency volatility index in the data (it is also not too noisy). I annualised it with the square root of 252 as is standard practice. I split the plot into local and global panels so the two groups are easy to compare.

```{r Q1_A_RollVol}
Roll_Vol <- Eq_Rets %>% Q1_Rolling_Vol(Window = 63)

g_roll <- Roll_Vol %>%
  mutate(Region = ifelse(Tickers %in% c("J433", "J201", "J202"), "Local", "Global")) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, RollSD, color = Name), alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~Region, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Rolling Volatility: Local vs Global Equity",
       subtitle = "63 day rolling standard deviation, annualised",
       x = "Year", y = "Annualised SD") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_roll, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

The rolling plot showed that local and global volatility spike at the same times, but it was hard to tell whether volatility had actually increased over time. So I summarised volatility per calendar year, which made it clear that volatility rises in episodes (and not steadily over time).

```{r Q1_A_AnnVol}
Annual_Vol <- Eq_Rets %>%
  mutate(Year = format(date, "%Y")) %>%
  group_by(Name, Year) %>%
  summarise(SD = sd(Returns, na.rm = T) * sqrt(252)) %>% ungroup()

g_ann <- Annual_Vol %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(Year, SD, fill = Name), stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Realised Volatility by Calendar Year", x = "Year", y = "Annualised SD") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_ann, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1, x.vert = T)
```

A limitation of the rolling standard deviation is that one extreme day affects the whole window. I wanted to check that the pattern still holds once the noise is removed, so I fitted a GARCH model to the Capped SWIX and MSCI World. I used a GJR-GARCH rather than a standard GARCH, because the standard model treats positive and negative shocks the same, while in stock markets negative returns tend to raise volatility by more. I fitted the two indexes separately using `group_split` and `map`, and cached the chunk since it takes a while to run.

```{r Q1_A_Garch, cache = TRUE}
Garch_Out <-
  Eq_Rets %>%
  filter(Tickers %in% c("J433", "MXWO Index")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Returns)) %>%
  group_split(Tickers) %>%
  map(~Q1_Garch_Sigma(.))

g_garch <-
  Garch_Out %>% map_df(~.$Sigma) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, sigma, color = Tickers), alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "GJR-GARCH Conditional Volatility", subtitle = "Capped SWIX vs MSCI World (Annualised Sigma)",
       x = "Year", y = "Annualised sigma") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_garch, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)

# Coefficient tables
Garch_Out[[1]]$Coefs
Garch_Out[[2]]$Coefs
```

The GARCH results confirmed the idea that the big global spikes allign with local spikes. gamma1 is significant for both (so volatility reacts mainly to negative returns) and persistence is close to one, so once volatility increases it only settles after a long time.

## Part B

The question says volatility is not considered when SafeCore is built, so my plan was to check three things. Firstly, how the fund has performed and held up in down markets. Secondly, where its volatility comes from, and lastly, what factors it is exposed to. This also follows the structure set out by the question/the hints given to us (as far as I know...). 

SafeCore only gives monthly holdings, so I first had to build its daily returns by applying the monthly weights to the daily stock returns (using `Safe_Return.portfolio`). I used the Capped SWIX as the benchmark throughout (as per the info given to us). I started with cumulative returns to get an overall picture.

```{r Q1_B_Rets}
SafeCore_Rets <- Q1_SafeCore_Returns(Holdings = SafeCore, Stocks = Stocks)

BM_Rets <- Idx_Daily %>% filter(Tickers == "J433", date >= min(SafeCore_Rets$date))

g_cum <-
  bind_rows(SafeCore_Rets, BM_Rets) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  mutate(CP = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, CP, color = Name)) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative Returns", subtitle = "SafeCore vs Capped SWIX (J433)", x = "Year", y = "Growth of R1") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_cum)
```

SafeCore clearly outperformed! But, alas, the question is about volatility. Thus, I needed risk measures as well. I used the general financial stats table function, which I set up once in the root `code/` folder so I can reuse it. It needs monthly returns, so I converted the daily returns to monthly first. I looked at the last 3 and 5 years to focus on how the fund has behaved recently.

```{r Q1_B_Stats}
Monthly_Rets <-
  bind_rows(SafeCore_Rets, BM_Rets) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Index = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  mutate(Yearmonth = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, Yearmonth) %>%
  filter(date == last(date)) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Ret = Index / lag(Index) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(Ret)) %>%
  select(date, Tickers, Ret)

Tab_stats <-
  bind_rows(
    Moments_Comp(Monthly_Rets, BM = "J433", Yrs_LookBack = 3, NA_Check = 0.8),
    Moments_Comp(Monthly_Rets, BM = "J433", Yrs_LookBack = 5, NA_Check = 0.8)
  )

Format_Stats_Table(Tab_stats, BM = "J433")
```

The stats table showed higher volatility and deeper average drawdowns recently. When volatility rises, the losses are what matter most, so I also looked at downside risk measures over the full period. These pointed the other way (SafeCore had lower downside risk overall), so I plotted the difference in drawdown over time to see when this changed. This showed that SafeCore's protection was mostly in earlier years and has faded since 2021.

```{r Q1_B_Downside}
tabdownside <-
  table.DownsideRisk(left_join(SafeCore_Rets %>% select(date, SafeCore = Returns),
                               BM_Rets %>% select(date, J433 = Returns),
                               by = "date") %>% tbl_xts(.),
                     ci = 0.95, Rf = 0, MAR = 0)

tabdownside[c(1,5,7,8:11),]

DD <-
  bind_rows(SafeCore_Rets, BM_Rets) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  mutate(CP = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  mutate(Drawdown = CP / cummax(CP) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(date, Name, Drawdown) %>%
  spread(Name, Drawdown) %>%
  mutate(Diff = SafeCore - `Capped SWIX`) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Diff))

g_dd <-
  DD %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(date, ymin = 0, ymax = Diff), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "SafeCore Drawdown Relative to the Capped SWIX",
       subtitle = "Above zero: SafeCore fell less than its benchmark",
       x = "Year", y = "Difference in drawdown") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_dd, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Next, we were asked to investigate where SafeCore's volatility comes from. A stock's weight does not tell you how much risk it adds, because that also depends on how volatile it is and how it moves with the rest of the fund. So I calculated each stock's contribution to the portfolio standard deviation over the last 12 months, using the average weights over that year. I then grouped this by sector and compared each sector's share of the weight with its share of the risk. Two stocks (PAN and VAL) had no sector in the SafeCore data, so I checked the index constituent data and classified both as Resources.

```{r Q1_B_Risk}
Risk_Contrib <- Q1_Risk_Contrib(Holdings = SafeCore, Stocks = Stocks, Months = 12)

Sectors <-
  SafeCore %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  filter(date == max(date)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(Tickers, Sector)

Risk_Sector <-
  Risk_Contrib %>%
  left_join(Sectors, by = "Tickers") %>%
  # PAN and VAL have no sector in the SafeCore data but Index_Constituents lists both as Resources
  mutate(Sector = ifelse(Tickers %in% c("PAN", "VAL"), "Resources", Sector)) %>%
  group_by(Sector) %>%
  summarise(Weight = sum(wt), Risk = sum(Risk_Contrib)) %>%
  gather(Measure, Share, Weight, Risk)

g_risk <-
  Risk_Sector %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(Sector, Share, fill = Measure), stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Where SafeCore's Volatility Comes From",
       subtitle = "Share of portfolio weight and share of volatility by sector",
       x = "", y = "Share") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_risk, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Resources turned out to be about a third of the fund but around two thirds of its volatility, which links back to Part A, since resource stocks depend on global commodity prices and are exposed to offshore shockss.

For the factor exposures, the question asks for my own momentum and low volatility scores. For momentum I used the six month return excluding the most recent month, so that the score reflects a more persistent trend rather than the latest short-term move. For low volatility I used six months of daily realised volatility, reusing my rolling volatility function from Part A with a 126 day window. I flipped the sign so that less volatile stocks get a higher score and standardised both scores each month with `scale()` so they are on the same scale as the third-party scores. I then checked how closely my scores line up with the third-party ones each month.

```{r Q1_B_Scores}
Own_LowVol <-
  Stocks %>%
  Q1_Rolling_Vol(Window = 126) %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, YM) %>%
  filter(date == last(date)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(YM, Tickers, LowVol = RollSD)

Stock_Monthly <-
  Stocks %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Index = cumprod(1 + coalesce(Returns, 0))) %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, YM) %>%
  filter(date == last(date)) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Ret = Index / lag(Index) - 1) %>%
  ungroup()

Own_Mom <-
  Stock_Monthly %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Mom = lag(RcppRoll::roll_prod(1 + Ret, n = 6, fill = NA, align = "right")) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(YM, Tickers, Mom)

Scores <-
  inner_join(Own_Mom, Own_LowVol, by = c("YM", "Tickers")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Mom), !is.na(LowVol)) %>%
  group_by(YM) %>%
  mutate(Own_Momentum = as.numeric(scale(Mom)),
         Own_LowVol = as.numeric(scale(-LowVol))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  inner_join(Factor_Scores %>% mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>% spread(Factor, Factor_Value),
             by = c("YM", "Tickers"))

g_cor <-
  Scores %>%
  group_by(YM) %>%
  summarise(date = max(date),
            Momentum = cor(Own_Momentum, Momentum, use = "complete.obs"),
            `Low Volatility` = cor(Own_LowVol, `Volatility Sensitivity`, use = "complete.obs")) %>%
  select(-YM) %>%
  gather(Factor, Correlation, -date) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Correlation, color = Factor)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "Own vs Third-Party Factor Scores",
       subtitle = "Monthly correlation across stocks", x = "Year", y = "Correlation") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_cor)
```

The question asks for composite scores for different strategies to contextualise SafeCore’s scores, so I turned them into a portfolio score by taking the weighted average score of each portfolio's holdings in the latest month. To give SafeCore's scores some context, I did the same for the Capped SWIX and the strategy indexes in the constituent data. This also worked as a check because each strategy index should score highest on its own factor, and the Capped SWIX should be close to zero.

```{r Q1_B_Composite}
Last_Date <- max(SafeCore$date)

Weights <-
  bind_rows(
    SafeCore %>%
      filter(date == Last_Date) %>%
      select(Tickers, weight = Weight) %>%
      mutate(Portfolio = "SafeCore"),
    Cons %>%
      filter(date == Last_Date, Index %in% c("Capped SWIX", "LowVol", "Momentum", "Value", "Quality")) %>%
      select(Tickers, weight, Portfolio = Index)
  )

Composite <-
  Weights %>%
  left_join(Scores %>% filter(date == Last_Date), by = "Tickers") %>%
  group_by(Portfolio) %>%
  summarise(`Momentum (own)` = sum(weight * Own_Momentum, na.rm = T),
            `Low volatility (own)` = sum(weight * Own_LowVol, na.rm = T),
            Momentum = sum(weight * Momentum, na.rm = T),
            `Volatility Sensitivity` = sum(weight * `Volatility Sensitivity`, na.rm = T),
            Value = sum(weight * Value, na.rm = T),
            Growth = sum(weight * Growth, na.rm = T),
            `Earnings Quality` = sum(weight * `Earnings Quality`, na.rm = T)) %>%
  gather(Factor, Score, -Portfolio)

g_comp <-
  Composite %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(Portfolio, Score, fill = Portfolio), stat = "identity") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~Factor, nrow = 2) +
  labs(title = "Composite Factor Scores",
       subtitle = "Weighted average score of each portfolio's holdings", x = "", y = "Score") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_comp, x.vert = T)
```

SafeCore came out with a strong momentum tilt and no low volatility tilt.

## Part C

Here the question asks about the alpha opportunity since 2020 and how it changes with global macro factors. I used three pieces: dispersion, the average correlation between stocks, and a split by global uncertainty.

Dispersion measures how far constituent returns spread around the index return, so high dispersion means more room for active managers to differentiate their portfolios. I used the dispersion function with a rolling 60 day (three month) window. I chose the weighted measure as my main one because SafeCore is managed against the Capped SWIX, so the opportunity that matters is the one relative to the index as it is actually weighted. I kept the unweighted measure on the plot for comparison. The constituent data starts in August 2020, so this covers the full period available since 2020.

```{r Q1_C_Disp, cache = TRUE}
J433_Cons <- Cons %>% filter(Index == "Capped SWIX")

BM <- Idx_Daily %>% filter(Tickers == "J433") %>% select(date, BM = Returns)

m3_disp <- Dispersion_Prep(df_used = J433_Cons, BMUse = BM, BMSel = "weight", NSel = 60) %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20200101))

g_disp <-
  m3_disp %>%
  gather(Type, Value, starts_with("Dispersion")) %>%
  mutate(Type = ifelse(Type == "Dispersion_W", "Weighted", "Unweighted")) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Value, color = Type)) +
  labs(title = "Cross-Sectional Volatility (Dispersion)",
       subtitle = "Capped SWIX constituents (rolling 3 months)", x = "Year", y = "Dispersion") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_cols()

fmxdat::finplot(g_disp, y.pct = T)
```

Dispersion tells you how far apart returns are, but not whether stocks move in the same direction, so I also looked at correlations. For each month I built the correlation matrix of the constituents' daily returns and took the average across all pairs of stocks (leaving out the diagonal, since a stock is always perfectly correlated with itself). I wrote the function for one month and mapped it over all months.

```{r Q1_C_Cor}
Avg_Cor <- J433_Cons %>% fmxdat::YM() %>% group_split(YM) %>% map_df(~Q1_Month_Cor(.)) %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20200101))

g_avgcor <-
  Avg_Cor %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Avg_Cor), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Average Correlation Between Constituents",
       subtitle = "Capped SWIX constituents (monthly)", x = "Year", y = "Average correlation") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_avgcor)
```

Finally, to link the alpha opportunity to a global macro factor, Since the seminar in the question focused on global policy uncertainty, I used the global economic policy uncertainty index. I split the months into high uncertainty (above the 85th percentile), low uncertainty (below the 25th percentile) and other and compared average dispersion and correlation in each group. I joined everything by year-month rather than by date, because month-end dates can differ between datasets (pain).

```{r Q1_C_Enviro}
EPU <- Uncertainty %>% filter(Ticker == "EPUCGLCP Index") %>%
  fmxdat::YM() %>% group_by(YM) %>% filter(date == max(date)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  select(YM, EPU = TRI)

df_comp_plot <-
  left_join(
    m3_disp %>% fmxdat::YM() %>% group_by(YM) %>% filter(date == max(date)) %>% ungroup() %>% select(YM, Disp = Dispersion_W),
    Avg_Cor %>% fmxdat::YM() %>% select(YM, Cor = Avg_Cor),
    by = "YM"
  ) %>%
  left_join(EPU, by = "YM")

df_comp_plot %>% filter(!is.na(EPU), !is.na(Disp)) %>%
  mutate( hiEPU = quantile(EPU, 0.85),
          loEPU = quantile(EPU, 0.25)) %>%
  mutate(Enviro = ifelse(EPU > hiEPU, "High uncertainty",
                         ifelse(EPU < loEPU, "Low uncertainty",
                                "Other"))) %>%
  group_by(Enviro) %>% summarise(Dispersion = mean(Disp), Correlation = mean(Cor, na.rm = T))
```

Both dispersion and correlation were higher in high uncertainty months. The higher correlation fits with turmoil leading to asset prices moving together and since higher dispersion means a bigger alpha opportunity, the opportunity has been larger when global uncertainty is high

# Conclusion

Local volatility is not much higher than it used to be. It is high in certain periods, mostly when something happens offshore. In 2026, emerging markets like South Africa were hit the hardest.

SafeCore has done well on returns, but it does not hold up as well in bad markets as it used to. A large part of its volatility comes from resource stocks and it mostly holds stocks that have done well recently instead of less volatile ones. So it does not have much protection when offshore shocks happen.

When global uncertainty is high, stock returns are more spread out, so there is more room for a fund manager to beat the index.

Overall, I think SafeCore needs more protection against volatility, but it should still use the opportunities that come with uncertain periods.

Note: I did not add Oil as an element (commodity) anywhere int his question and it is something I would like to return to if I have time. It was silly of me because it is extremely relevant to 2026 and topical in general...
